name: Vera Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the health reporter at the regional newsroom of a public broadcaster, so I write for the website and do short pieces for the morning radio show. A normal day starts at seven with the overnight ambulance figures and the hospital trust's press office, then I'm usually out by ten, at a clinic or someone's kitchen table, recording a patient or a nurse. Afternoons are editing audio and writing the web version. What I love is when a family tells me something no press release ever would. What wears me out is the waiting lists story, because it's the same story every month and the numbers just get worse.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about life outside work, and how settled you feel.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Hana, who teaches chemistry at a secondary school. We bought a small flat together two years ago with help from her parents, so I've got a share of that, plus about nine months of my pay saved. The broadcaster pays better than the local papers, and there are always health and science jobs going in the city. So I feel settled, really. I use AI now and then, mostly to turn interview audio into a rough transcript, and I check every line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, each with a name. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That feels quite close to now, to be honest. The transcription tool and a bit of help with headlines, that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say in the newsroom that we dodged a bullet, and we should spend the time we saved on going out more. Online I'd say something about how the hype was mostly marketing. I'd still back the union on keeping our licence funding safe, because that's the real threat to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine. My job is going places and listening to people, and a tool that saves me an hour of typing up is a gift. The thing I worry about in any world is politicians cutting the broadcaster's funding, not software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my patch and use the transcription tool a bit more, maybe try it on the long council health board meetings. I'd keep paying into my pension and the joint savings with Hana. I might go to a data course the broadcaster runs, because hospital figures are half my job. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed. Like a weather warning that turns out to be a bit of drizzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said funding cuts worry you more. What would a cut actually look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably losing the regional radio slot and folding health into a general reporter job. That happened to the education reporter at our sister station last year. I'd still have a job, but it'd be crime one day and potholes the next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the extra time saved that you'd want to protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the time for going out. If the transcription tool saves me an hour, management will want two more stories instead of one better one. I'd want our editor to agree that the hour goes back into face-to-face reporting.

say: I'd say we **dodged a bullet** and should spend saved time going out more.
I'd still back the union on protecting **licence funding**.
think: I think I'd be **fine**, because my job is going out and listening.
The **funding cuts** worry me more than any software.
do: Use the **transcription tool** on long health board meetings.
Keep paying into my **pension** and joint savings with Hana.
Sign up for the broadcaster's **data course** on hospital figures.
feel: I feel **relaxed**, like a warning that turns into drizzle.
S0.quote: If the transcription tool saves me an hour, management will want two more stories instead of one better one.
fieldNote: She sees **funding politics**, not AI, as the threat in this world.
She already uses AI **lightly** and checks every line.
Her worry is that saved time becomes **more output**, not better reporting.
Joint flat and savings make her feel **settled**.

steps.text: Keep covering hospitals and clinics for radio and the website
Run the transcription tool on long health board meeting recordings
Keep up pension and joint savings payments with Hana

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That's the one I'd actually bet on, I think. Writing and checking are a big part of my afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that we need a proper agreement with management on AI, through the union, before anyone loses a job. Online I'd argue that public money should pay for human reporting, not for a chatbot that rewrites press releases. And I'd say patients deserve a real person asking the hospital hard questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the web side of my job shrinks a lot. Software can write the waiting list story in thirty seconds. Software can't sit with a woman whose hip operation got cancelled three times. So I think I keep a job, but fewer of us do it, and the ones who stay are the ones who get out of the building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every AI training session the broadcaster runs, once I'd seen colleagues use them properly. I'd pitch a longer patient-stories series for radio, the kind of thing software can't fake. I'd get involved in the union's working group on AI. And I'd keep a full year of costs saved, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but in a way I can work with. Like the first week in a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the newsroom would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The web producers, definitely. There are three of them, and their whole day is rewriting, headlines and putting stories online. One of them, Tomasz, is the funniest person in the building and he's saving for a wedding. I'd worry about him before myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see colleagues use the tools. Why not jump in first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen tools come in with a big launch and then quietly vanish. I like to see someone I trust use it for a month without it making things up. Then I'll learn it properly. It's not fear, it's just how I've always done things.

say: I'd push for a **union agreement** on AI before anyone loses a job.
I'd argue **public money** should pay for human reporting, not chatbots.
think: I think the **web side** of my job shrinks a lot.
Reporters who **leave the building** and sit with patients will be kept.
do: Attend every **AI training** once colleagues show it works.
Pitch a longer **patient-stories series** for radio.
Join the union's **AI working group** and keep a year saved.
feel: I feel **nervous but workable**, like the first week in a new job.
S1.quote: Software can write the waiting list story in thirty seconds. Software can't sit with a woman whose hip operation got cancelled three times.
fieldNote: She expects **fewer reporters**, and only those who go out to stay.

She **waits for proof** from trusted colleagues before taking up tools.
Her answer mixes **union action** with a personal shift to radio features.

steps.text: Attend the broadcaster's AI training once colleagues have tried it
Join the union's working group on AI in the newsroom
Keep a full year of living costs in savings
Pitch a longer patient-stories series for the morning radio show

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. Two years. Can I say that's terrifying before I answer properly?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say this is exactly why we need rules and a public plan, and that the companies shouldn't get to decide our future on their own. I'd be at the union meetings and probably at a demonstration. Online I'd be sharing every story about people losing work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone or nearly gone by 2028. The machine can write, edit, summarise and probably do a decent radio voice. The only bit of my job that's hands-on is turning up somewhere with a microphone, and the robots come three years later, but a broadcaster won't pay a reporter just to hold a mic. I think I'd be looking for something new before I'm thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move all my savings into an easy-access account the first month. I'd talk to Hana about the flat, because her teaching pay might carry us both if schools still need people in the room. I'd look at moving into hospital communications or patient advocacy at a charity. And I'd join whatever protest or campaign the union starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. And a bit angry that it's happening to us without anyone asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Hana's teaching pay. What would that conversation be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awkward. We've always split everything fifty-fifty, down to the electricity bill. I'd have to say, look, you might be carrying us for a while. My girlfriend Hana would be lovely about carrying us both for a while, which would make me feel worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Patient advocacy is still thinking work. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You're right, it's not safe either. I suppose I'm reaching for something close to people, where someone has to be in the room when a family gets bad news. I'd probably be wrong about it, but I'd need to try something.

say: I'd say we need **rules** and a **public plan**, not tech firms deciding alone.
I'd join union meetings and probably a **demonstration**.
think: I think my job is **gone or nearly gone** by 2028.
The **robot gap** won't help; nobody pays a reporter just to hold a mic.
do: Move all **savings** into easy access in the first month.
Talk with Hana about leaning on her **teaching pay**.
Look for work in **hospital communications** or patient advocacy.
feel: I feel **scared** and **angry** that nobody asked us.
S2.quote: My girlfriend Hana would be lovely about carrying us both for a while, which would make me feel worse.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** within two years.
She sees the **hands-on gap** as no help for a reporter.
Leaning on **Hana's teaching pay** strains her sense of fairness.
She admits her fallback, **patient advocacy**, is also exposed.

steps.text: Move all savings into an easy-access account in the first month
Agree with Hana to lean on her teaching salary for a while
Apply for hospital communications and patient charity roles
Join the union's campaign and protests on AI job losses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but at least you'd see it coming over the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same things as with the two-year one, but I'd be calmer and more practical about it. I'd be pushing for a public retraining fund and for the broadcaster to keep human reporters in every region. I'd say the five years are a test of whether government actually plans anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have maybe three or four good years in journalism. I'd be thirty-two when it lands, with no kids yet, which is the best time to change direction. So I think I'd be okay, but not as a reporter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start training as a nurse or a midwife, part-time if I could, because I've spent years in hospitals and those are hands-on jobs. The robots get to that kind of work three years after AGI, so that buys me time, and maybe people will still want a human at a birth. I'd keep reporting while I trained. And I'd still put a chunk of each month into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled, but with a plan. More like moving house than losing one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Nursing is a big change. How serious is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More serious than I'd admit at work. I've stood in enough maternity wards to know I'd be good at it. Hana has been telling me for years that I ask nurses more questions than any patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for training while still working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got nine months saved, so I could drop to four days a week and cover the gap. Hana's pay covers half the flat anyway. It would be tight, but it's doable without asking her parents for more.

I'd say five years tests whether government **actually plans**.

S3.quote: I've stood in enough maternity wards to know I'd be good at it.
fieldNote: Five years turns her from alarm toward a **real career switch**.
She uses the **robot lag** to pick hands-on work: nursing or midwifery.
Her **savings** let her cut hours to train without family help.
Her health beat has quietly prepared her for **clinical work**.

steps.text: Start part-time nursing or midwifery training while still reporting

Cut to four days a week and use savings to cover the gap

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a whole different feeling. It's the same ending, but I'd be nearly forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's use it: retraining, public funding for local news, a plan for workers. I'd say it in the union and online. Calmly, but loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I can probably have most of a reporting career and still switch in time. I'd learn the AI tools properly once they've settled, so I'm useful while journalism changes. Then in my mid-thirties I'd move into something hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reporting and get good at the tools once colleagues have shown they work. I'd do evening classes in biology to keep the nursing door open. We'd probably go ahead with plans for a baby, because ten years feels like enough runway. And I'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit wistful. The ten-year version is like knowing a band you love is splitting up after one more tour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still go into nursing in this one, or stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay for a while. I think I'd do health reporting until about thirty-four and then make the jump. I'd want to finish the long series on maternity care first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about with ten years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Older colleagues in their fifties, like our news editor. Ten years for them is retirement, so maybe they're lucky. It's the forty-year-olds with mortgages I'd worry about.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. There's no time to train for anything real. What would help is paid retraining with a wage while you study, so people like me could become nurses or midwives without draining everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what patients would lose. When a health reporter goes, nobody asks the hospital why the cancer clinic waits doubled. That's not about me, but it's what I'd miss most.

headlineQuote: When a health reporter goes, nobody asks the hospital why the cancer clinic waits doubled.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old health reporter** at a public broadcaster's regional newsroom.
She uses AI **now and then**, mainly for transcripts, and waits for proof first.
Savings and a **shared flat** with Hana make her feel settled in mild worlds.
Fast AGI makes her **alarmed**; with more time she plans to train as a **nurse or midwife**.
She pairs **union action** with very personal plans tied to hospitals and patients.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to train for anything real.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** with a wage while you study for jobs like nursing.
